Bathsheba was the wife of Uriah the Hittite who became the mother of Solomon after King David seduced her and orchestrated her husband's death. She was the daughter of Eliam and a trusted general's wife. David saw her bathing, desired her, and summoned her to his palace. She became pregnant with his child. To cover up the affair, David ordered Uriah's death in battle by positioning him in the fiercest fighting, then took Bathsheba as his wife. When the prophet Nathan confronted David with a parable, condemning his sin, God struck down the illegitimate child as punishment. Solomon, their second son, was born after David's repentance and became David's chosen successor, despite being younger than his brothers. Bathsheba acted as queen mother and advocated powerfully for Solomon at court, ensuring his rightful ascension to the throne despite rival claims. Her story illustrates the complex intersection of royal power, morality, and redemption. David's most grievous sin paradoxically produced the greatest and wisest king of Israel's entire dynasty.
